string.text: {=taom_str_culture_description.empire}The Dunlendings are a proud and ancient folk of the White Mountains and the wild hills of Dunland. Long before the coming of Númenórean lords or the gift of Calenardhon to the House of Eorl, their forefathers roamed the valleys between Isen and Adorn. Much of their bitterness stems from this memory. They have not forgotten what was taken, nor who it was given to. Clannish and fiercely independent, the Dunlendings dwell in timber halls and hill-forts, bound tightly by blood and oath. They are herdsmen, hunters and raiders in equal measure. Suspicious of strangers and openly hostile toward Rohan, many among them have at times heeded the whispers of darker powers, if only to reclaim what they believe was stolen. Yet they are not servants by nature. Their loyalty is to kin and chieftain alone. To underestimate the Dunlendings as mere brigands is folly. They know every vale and ridge of their land, and when united beneath a strong war-leader, they are capable of far more than border skirmishes. Old grudges die hard in Dunland and the hills remember.

{=taom_str_culture_description.vlandia}Rohan, Land of the Horselords and of much contention. Claimed as rightful homeland by not one, but three kinships of Men, Rohan or Calenardhon, as it was called under Gondorian rule, was given to Eorl the Young as a reward for his military assistance to Gondor in the wars of the past. From then onwards, the House of Eorl has steadily ruled the land between the Anduin and the Isen. The Men of Rohan, the Rohirrim, are steadfast, distrusting of strangers and highly pastoral. Many of them live scattered around the Mark, in small villages or farms of their own. Big towns are seldomly seen in Rohan. Though, even with this scattered and divided way of living, the Rohirrim and the Eótheod are greatly proud of their land and of the deeds that won it - and will defend against anything and anyone. Few things mean more to Rohan than the keeping of Oaths, their horses and the loyalty to their friends.

{=taom_str_culture_description.battania}The Variags of Khand dwell in the dry uplands and wind-swept plains east of Mordor, a hard people shaped by harsher lands. Little given to grand cities or monuments, they favor fortified camps, caravan strongholds and mobile war-bands that can vanish as swiftly as they appear. Horsemen first and foremost, the Variags prize speed, discipline and decisive violence. Their warriors ride lean steppe-bred mounts, clad in layered leathers and scale, wielding recurved bows and curved blades with equal skill. Trade routes from Near Harad and Rhûn pass through their territories, and the Variags have long learned that tolls and tribute may be as profitable as plunder. Pragmatic rather than devout, they have often marched beneath the banners of greater powers when it suited them - Mordor most notably - yet their loyalty is measured in advantage, not reverence. The Variags remember every slight and repay debts in kind, whether in silver or in blood. In times of war, their cavalry can strike like a desert storm: sudden, blinding and gone before resistance can gather.

{=taom_str_culture_description.khuzait}The Easterlings of Rhûn hail from the vast and varied lands beyond the Sea of Rhûn, where steppe, river-valley and gilded city meet. Chief among their realms is the Medlóshukain - a dominion of wealth, pageantry and disciplined might. Unlike the scattered tribes that wander the eastern plains, the people of the Medlóshukain maintain ordered cities of obsidian and jade, their rulers adorned in gold and silk. Great roads bind their territories together, and caravans heavy with spice, metal and fine craft pass beneath banners bright as the rising sun. Their armies are no rabble host: shielded infantry, chariots and armored horsemen march in measured ranks, drilled for cohesion and spectacle alike. Long have they looked westward - sometimes as traders, often as conquerors. Alliances with darker powers have come and gone through the centuries, for the lords of Rhûn are ambitious above all else. Yet to mistake them as mere pawns of Mordor is folly. The Golden Realm acts in its own interest, and its pride is ancient. When the hosts of Rhûn ride to war, they do so not only for shadow - but for glory, dominion and the expansion of their ever-shining horizon.

{=taom_str_culture_description.aserai}The Haruze are the product of the constant intermingling of many different tribes of Harad for over 2000 years. For much of their history, their land, which they call Harwan, was splintered and divided into a multitude of different kingdoms. Though now, after the coming of Sûladan, the Black Serpent, an empire has been established, that had not been seen by the Haruze in over 300 years. Many of them are simple herders and oasis farmers, able to traverse the deadly Dune Sea with ease and at great speed. Their pack animals and their horses they call 'Târag', meaning 'Windwalkers'. And like the wind their cavalry and their light infantry can wash over entire armies of the enemy. And enemy, that was formerly Sauron, but has, in more recent years, often been Gondor. Highly and deeply connected to their land, the Haruze lay claim to all of Harad and have long-since been eyeing the fertile coastlands of Harondor. A land fit for the taking, now that Gondor has waned.

{=taom_str_culture_description.sturgia}The Dalríngi, or simply 'Dalemen', are the inhabitants of the great northern realm of Men. Due to the heroics of one of their own kind, Bard the Bowman, they are also sometimes referred to as 'Bardings'. Mercantile and highly crafty in nature, much wealth has flown through Dale, and the surrounding lands, including the great dwarven realm of Erebor and the Eryn Lasgalen under the steadfast rule of Thranduil has flurished. After the death of Smaug and the rebuilding of Dale, the Dalríngi have once again re-established themselves as great traders, marksmen and able sailors. Their lands now stretch from the Withered Approach in the north into the western reaches of Rhûn. Friendly to most of their neighbors, though distrustful of some, the Dalemen are a good friend to have, in times when friends grow rare.

{=taom_str_culture_description.erebor}Durin's Folk. The most well known clan of the dwarves, the Longbeards are once again on the rise towards the zenith of their power. After the death of the dragon under the Lonely Mountain and the ascension of Dáin Ironfoot to King, the Iron Hills have been integrated into the Kingdom of Erebor. Though the true treasure of their kind is not the Lonely Mountain, the Arkenstone or their ancient heritage - but Khazad-dûm. Moria, as it is now called, has long been the golden apple for the Longbeards and efforts have been made in the past to reclaim the ancient capital of their people. Spread across the eastern bounds of the Ered Mithrin, the Longbeards have established friendships with the Elves of Mirkwood, the Men of Dale and the Avari of Neldoreth. As long as coin keeps flowing into their purses, the Gates of Erebor will stay open and the land will thrive.

{=taom_str_culture_description.rivendell}The Noldor of Lindon and Imladris are among the last of the High Elves remaining in Middle-earth. Once mighty princes of Beleriand and jewel-smiths without equal, they now dwell in fading havens west of the Misty Mountains, their glory tempered by sorrow. In Lindon, beneath the watch of the Grey Havens, they maintain what remains of their ancient realms - dignified, restrained and ever mindful of the Sea. In Rivendell, wisdom rather than power defines them. Lore, memory and quiet vigilance are their chosen pursuits. The fire that once drove them across the Helcaraxë burns lower now, yet it has not gone out entirely. Proud but no longer wrathful, the Noldor have learned hard lessons. They are courteous to allies, distant to strangers and implacable to enemies. Though the world of Men waxes and their own wanes, the Noldor endure as stewards of memory, a memory that is not easily extinguished.

{=taom_str_culture_description.mirkwood}The Silvan Elves of Mirkwood are a woodland folk in the truest sense. Less concerned with what goes on in the south and the west, they are hunters, foresters and wardens of Greenwood the Great. Under the rule of the great King Thranduil, the Silvan elves have grown more structured, though they retain their rustic heart. They favor strong drink, hearty feasts and skilled archery. Their halls beneath the forest are less concerned with grandeur than with defense and practicality. Having endured the shadow of Dol Guldur and the creeping corruption of their woods, the Silvan Elves are wary and resolute. They are slower to trust than many of their kindred - but once given, their friendship is steadfast and long lasting. Just like their forests.

{=taom_str_culture_description.lothlorien}The Sindar of Lothlórien dwell beneath golden leaves and timeless boughs. Though ruled by Galadriel of the Noldor and Celeborn of Doriath, the woodland realm is largely Silvan and Sindarin in custom, blending ancient forest life with the echoes of long lost Beleriand. Graceful and contemplative, the Sindar of Lórien are less restless than their western kin. They seek preservation over departure and healing over memory. Within the eaves of their guarded land, time itself seems reluctant to pass. Song and quiet watchfulness define their days. Yet beneath their serenity lies vigilance. None cross the borders of Lórien unseen, and few depart unchanged. Though they desire no glory or might, they will defend their Golden Wood with a resolve as deep as its roots.

{=taom_str_culture_description.isengard}The Uruk-hai are the pinnacle of Orc-kind’s breeding, wrought for war and discipline. Larger, stronger and more enduring beneath the sun than lesser Orcs, they were fashioned to be soldiers first and foremost. Unlike the rabble of the Misty Mountains, the Uruk-hai fight in ordered companies, bearing heavy shields and iron helms marked with the sigil of their master. Loyalty among them is born not of affection, but of fear and ambition. Strength commands obedience; weakness invites death. Efficient and relentless, the Uruk-hai are less prone to bickering than their lesser kin, though treachery remains ever present. Where they march, they do so not for plunder alone, but for conquest and slaughter. Conquest, slaughter and to end the Age of Men, before it can begin.

{=taom_str_culture_description.gundabad}The Orcs of Mount Gundabad are among the oldest tribes of their kind in the North. Long entrenched in the roots of the Misty Mountains, they claim ancient dominion over its passes and peaks. Hardy and numerous, they thrive in cold caverns and high crags. Unlike the more regimented hosts of Mordor, the Gundabad Orcs favor strength of numbers and savage assault. Their hatred for Dwarves burns brightest, for Gundabad itself is a place of ancient grievance. When united beneath a powerful chieftain, such as Azog and Bolg in the past, they can flood from the mountains in terrifying force. The North has known their fury before, and remembers it still.

{=taom_str_culture_description.umbar}The people of Umbar are the heirs of a divided legacy. Founded as a proud haven of Númenórean mariners in the South, Umbar once rivaled Pelargir in splendor and ambition. Yet where Pelargir remained faithful to the West, Umbar turned - first in pride, and later in open defiance. A seafaring people above all else, the Umbareans command swift corsair fleets that prowl the coasts from Harondor to Belfalas. Their harbors are deep, their shipyards ever busy, and their captains as bold as they are ruthless. Trade and piracy walk hand in hand in Umbar, and few vessels pass the Bay of Belfalas without paying heed to its black-sailed ships. Proud of their Númenórean descent yet scornful of Gondor’s claim to it, the Umbareans measure worth in strength and dominance. Feuds with the Dúnedain of the North and South run deep, fed by centuries of rivalry and bloodshed. Though diminished from their ancient height, Umbar remains dangerous — for its people have never forgotten how to rule the sea, nor how to make war upon those who would deny their claim as the heirs of Castamir.

{=taom_str_culture_description.dolguldur}The minions of Dol Guldur, under the command of the Necromancer, are a dark and sinister force. Hidden within the corrupted forest of Mirkwood, they employ treachery and shadow to weaken their enemies. Orcs, wargs, and other foul creatures march forth to spread fear and decay across Middle-earth.

{=taom_str_culture_description.gondor}The Men of Gondor, the Land of Stone, are among the last remaining remnants of old Númenor. Albeit far diminished from their ancient sires Elendil, Isildur and Anarión, they and their leaders, the Ruling Stewards in Minas Tirith, are a hardy folk. Often hard-pressed by the ever watchful shadow in the East, many lands formerly of Gondor are now under the control of the Haradrim or the Easterlings. Most costly of these losses however was that of Minas Ithil, now fashioned Minas Morgul, in T.A. 2002. Since then and since the Great Plague that swept through much of Ithilien and Anórien, the Gondorians have turned inward. Many of them live in the rolling hills of Lamedon or along the glimmering coastline of Anfalas, far removed from any threat and danger, working as traders, craftsmen, loremasters or sailors. Though, should the need arise, and the Stewards call upon the fiefdoms, their call to war will be answered. Gondor may be waning, but it is not weak.

{=taom_str_culture_description.mordor}The Orcs of Mordor are as harsh and varied as the land that birthed them. Drawn from many breeds and tribes, they gather beneath the Dark Tower in uneasy unity. Cruel, cunning and ever watchful for advantage, these Orcs survive through brutality and hierarchy. Captains rule through terror, and alliances shift with the promise of favor. Though often fractious, they are bound together by fear of a greater power - and that fear keeps them in line. Accustomed to ash-choked skies and barren plains, they are hardened beyond most of their kind. In siege and attrition, they excel. The Black Land shapes its children well.

AI realms keep their own rules either way. Applies at once, no restart. This is the default for new campaigns. With the Alignment rules start option on Standard, a campaign follows this switch live; Strict or Relaxed fixes all four alignment switches for that campaign. Older saves follow this setting.

{=taom_str_culture_description.abanissa}The Jármata of Âbanissa are not the native inhabitants of their land. Standing as the westernmost realm of Far Harad, Âbanissa has enjoyed enormous prosperity, pomp, decadence, military might and splendor. Its location along the richest trade route in all of the Middle-earth, the Great Ivory Road, has enabled Âbanissa and the native Âbakhâna to enforce tolls and taxes on all trade between the westlands of Middle-earth and the Bay of Ormal, laying just south of them. Though, this wealth attracted the Jármata, a warlike and ruthless tribal confederation from the East. The Jármata, like most people of Far Harad, are pragmatic. They will not side with anyone, even their friends, if the chances of winning are not high enough. Envious of the Shaghâni and their long heritage, the Jármata have often tried to encroach on the central Dune Sea and frequently find themselves at odds with their neighbors. A state of affairs, many of their kind seem to enjoy.

{=taom_str_culture_description.shaghana}The Shaghâni are perhaps the most learned folk in all of Middle-earth. Greatly priding themselves on their ancient capital of Zajâna, with its blue towers and houses of wisdom, the Shaghâni stand as a buffer between the faithful realm of Bellakar in its northward expedition and the mighty Âbanissa, richest and most powerful of the kingdoms of Far Harad - or Jármat, as the Shaghâni call it. Renowned for their prowess in mounted combat, the Shaghâni are feared across the Dune Sea for their camel cavalry. Screamers is what many of the Haradrim call those units and even Âbanissa, in all its splendor and might, would do good in leaving the Shaghâni to their own devices. For that is all the Shaghâni want - To be left alone and to be left unincumbered by a war far to the north. A north, they care little about.

{=taom_shaghana_desc}Shaghâna is the eastern reach of Harad, a land of sun-scorched steppes and ancient fortresses. Its nine tribal clans are fierce warriors, bound together by oath and blood, striking fear into those who dare oppose them.

{=aom_shaghana_desc}The Shaghâna are a fierce tribal people of the eastern Harad steppes, renowned as relentless raiders and skilled horsemen. Bound by oath and clan, they answer to their Taskral and serve the dark designs of Sauron from their sun-scorched fortresses.

{=taom_abanissa_desc}Âbanissa lies in the deep south of Harad, a realm of humid jungles and ancient stone dynasties. The great Houses of Âbanissa command fearsome war-beasts and armies of disciplined warriors, their power answerable to none but Sauron himself.

{=aom_abanissa_desc}The great Houses of Âbanissa rule the deep south of Harad, a land of humid jungles, ancient stone palaces and towering war-beasts. Their armies march beneath banners of dynasty, commanding respect and terror across the southern lands.

{=TAOM_ghilman_text}The Serpent Guard are mounted soldiers in the service of the Serpentlord of Near Harad. Bred in the saddle on the rolling plains south of the Ephel Dúath, they are unmatched as horse-archers in all of Middle-earth's southern lands. In times of peace between Harad and Mordor, the Guard hires its services to Haradrim lords and to any other power rich enough to afford their golden fee.

{=TAOM_legion_text}The Grey Company are the last organised brotherhood of the Dúnedain Rangers, descendants of the kings of Arnor who lost their kingdom ages ago. They ride across the North without a home of their own, keeping the peace in lands that have forgotten their names. Though their first loyalty is to the line of Elendil, they take contracts from lords across Middle-earth when their wandering brings them through civilised lands.

{=TAOM_skolderbrotva_text}The Axemen of Erebor are veterans of King Thorin's battles who found peacetime ill-suited to their temperament. Trained in the close-quarter fighting of the Dwarven halls — shield wall, short axe, mattock — they are formidable on any terrain but excel in the mountain passes that connect Erebor to the kingdoms of men. They take contracts from any who can afford their fee, but will not raise an axe against Erebor or Rivendell.

{=TAOM_company_text}The Corsair Blades are veteran sea-fighters from the harbours of Umbar who have taken to selling their skills on land. They fight as crossbowmen — the preferred arm of shipboard warfare — and are as comfortable in a siege as they are on a rolling deck. Their captain, a scarred Númenórean exile, keeps them to their contracts with iron discipline, knowing that their reputation is their most valuable cargo.

{=TAOM_beni_zilal_text}The Blind Eye is a brotherhood of smugglers, fences, and hired killers operating across the coasts of Harad and the deep desert. They are said to descend from a cult of assassins who served a forgotten Haradrim king, and their methods — poison, shadow, and the leveraging of secrets — remain unchanged. Lords who wish to quietly remove a rival, or merchants who need cargo moved without customs inspection, know where to leave a gold coin and a sealed letter.

{=TAOM_wolfskins_text}The Variag Ravagers are war-bands of young Variag warriors from the steppes of Khand who spend their early manhood in a state of ritual warfare: they may own no cooked food, sleep under no permanent roof, and take no mercy. While most eventually return to the settled life of their clans, some never do, and these form the Ravagers — outlaws who prey on the roads of Khand and raid across its borders into Harad and Gondor.

{=TAOM_brotherhood_text}The Dunlending Reavers are the broken remnant of a hill-clan that once dwelt in the valleys now ruled by the Rohirrim. Their grandfathers were driven from fertile land into the rocky heights, and they have nursed that bitterness into a raider's philosophy: everything taken from a southron or a king's man is merely the restoration of what was stolen. In practice they are brigands, but dangerous ones who know every goat-track through the hills.

{=TAOM_hidden_hand_text}The Mouth's Servants are the Eyes of Barad-dûr operating beyond the Black Gate — informants, enforcers, and spies embedded among the peoples bordering Mordor. Where Sauron's armies cannot yet reach, these agents collect tribute and silence dissent. They work through bribery, blackmail, and quiet murder, ensuring that no conspiracy against the Dark Lord takes root before it is uprooted and crushed.

{=TAOM_lakepike_text}The Wreckers of the Long Lake live in the reed-beds and rotting old jetties of the Long Lake's shadowed shores, far from the respectable lights of Esgaroth. They make their living by luring barges onto hidden shoals with false lanterns, then stripping the cargo and selling it through fences in the town itself. Despite the efforts of the Lake-town Master and the Dale merchants, the Wreckers have too many friends in the dockside taverns to be easily driven out.

{=TAOM_embers_text}The Cult of the Lidless Eye is a secret society rooted in the Black Númenórean tradition, venerating Sauron as a god-king who will restore his faithful to glory when he rises again. They recruit among the dispossessed of Dunland and the forgotten corners of the realm, promising divine favour and earthly power. In truth, their leaders answer to agents of Barad-dûr, and their cell-based structure makes them nearly impossible for any lord's justice to eradicate.

{=TAOM_jawwal_text}The Sand-Riders are the nomadic desert clans of the deep Harad interior, masters of the waterless wastes between the Ephel Dúath and the distant southern sea. They range across routes known only to themselves, demanding tribute from any caravan bold enough to cross their territory. The settled lords of Near Harad treat them as a nuisance; the Sand-Riders consider the settled lords thieves who stole what the desert had already given freely.

{=TAOM_karakhuzaits_text}The Wild Easterlings are the unconquered steppe clans of the Sea of Rhûn, who have resisted the authority of every lord who has tried to bring them to heel — Rhûn chieftain, Mordor lieutenant, and King of Dale alike. They range across the grasslands east of the Celduin, rounding up horses, raiding flocks, and collecting road tribute from any caravan foolish enough to cross their steppe without an armed escort.

{=TAOM_forest_people_text}The Drúedain, known to Men as Woses or the Wild Men of the Woods, are an ancient people who dwell in the deep forest of Drúadan and the hidden valleys of the White Mountains. They clear ground with fire, grow what they need on the ash-rich soil, and move on when the land is spent — a way of life the settled peoples of Middle-earth have never understood and never bothered to. The Drúedain want no lord, pay no tax, and ask only to be left to the forest's silence.

{=TAOM_eleftheroi_text}The Beornings are the great woodmen who dwell in the vale of the Anduin between the Misty Mountains and Mirkwood, led by the skin-changers of Beorn's line. They allow no Orc to cross their territory, charge a toll at the Ford of Carrock to fund their watch, and answer to no king in Middle-earth. Though they will trade and talk with Elves and Dwarves, any army that marches through their forest without leave will find that the Beornings have very large teeth.

{=taom_precompile_hint}Pre-compiles the troop and equipment shaders so first battles do not stutter or stall. Re-run after any change to your mod list: the game clears its compiled shaders when the module list changes.

{=taom_precompile_inquiry_body}Loads a series of hidden battles containing the troops, lords and battle equipment of TAOM and the base game, so their shaders are compiled now instead of during your first battle against each culture.{newline}{newline}This takes a while: expect 20 to 70 minutes on a fresh shader cache. Leave the game running and do not start another battle; progress shows on the loading screen and as a status line. Hold Ctrl+Shift+K at any time to cancel.{newline}{newline}The game clears its compiled shaders whenever your module list changes, so run this again after adding, removing or reordering mods.{newline}{newline}Scene passes (terrain and atmosphere shaders for TAOM's own battle scenes) are off by default because they crash some GPUs. Turn them on under Mod Options, TAOM, Graphics/Shader Precompilation if you want them.{newline}{newline}When you see 'Shader pre-compilation COMPLETE', you can play.

{=taom_career_switch_no_targets}No eligible careers available for your culture and standing.

{=taom_cq_capt_osg_t2_desc}Osgiliath's ruins must hold against the Shadow. Prove yourself worthy of the rank of Captain — win Gondor's battles, master the blade, and let your renown spread along the Anduin.
{=taom_hideout_desc_dunland}Among the wooded hills of Dunland you spy a rough camp of hide tents and a crude palisade, half-hidden in a clearing.
{=taom_hideout_desc_gundabad}Beneath the crags of the Misty Mountains you find a foul warren of Gundabad orcs burrowed into the bare rock.
{=taom_hideout_desc_feral_orcs}Deep in a scarred hollow of the wilds you find a ragged den of feral orcs, ringed with gnawed bones and stolen iron.
{=taom_hideout_desc_harad}Out among the dunes of Harad you come upon a camouflaged Southron camp gathered about a hidden desert well.
{=taom_hideout_desc_rhun}On the wide grasslands of Rhûn you make out the wagons and hide-tents of an Easterling raiding band camped in a gully.
{=taom_hideout_desc_umbar}Along the southern shore you find a sheltered cove where the black ships of the Corsairs of Umbar lie at anchor.
{=taom_hideout_desc_erebor}Among the bleak hills of the east you come upon a dwarf-camp of the Blacklocks, a clan long ago fallen into shadow and ruin.

{=taom_faction_anduin_vale_desc}The Beornings and the Woodmen of the Vales hold the upper Anduin between the Misty Mountains and Mirkwood, with the Carrock and the Old Ford as their keys. Farmers, herdsmen and honey-keepers, they stand apart from the War of the Ring, but the orcs and wolves of the mountains test their few halls every year.
{=taom_faction_anduin_vale_bonus_1}-0.5 settlement loyalty per day (Small Territory Exposure)
{=taom_faction_anduin_vale_perk_0_desc}+10% party speed on plains, the open river meadows the folk of the vales know best.
{=taom_faction_anduin_vale_perk_1_desc}Stands outside the War of the Ring: no alliance and no sworn enemy at the start of a campaign.
{=taom_faction_anduin_vale_strength_0}A strong axe line, from the Beorning Youth to the Bear-warden
{=taom_faction_anduin_vale_strength_2}No sworn enemy at the start of a campaign
{=taom_faction_anduin_vale_weakness_2}Orcs and wolves of the Misty Mountains at the door
{=taom_faction_aru_thani_of_bellakar_desc}The coastal realm of Bellakar, settled by Numenorean Faithful who remained true to the Valar. A bastion of civilization on the southern shores.
{=taom_faction_clans_of_dunland_bonus_0}50% less forest speed penalty + 15% sight range (Woodland Upbringing)
{=taom_faction_clans_of_dunland_bonus_4}+20% chance for veteran militia in towns (Hardened Hillfolk)

{=taom_faction_clans_of_dunland_desc}The Hill-Men of Dunland, ancient enemies of the Rohirrim. Generations in the deep woods and high moors shaped the Hill Marchers and Hill-Tribe Levies, cheap, fast, angry warbands that march on plain and forest alike. Their smiths are slow, but their warbands are not.
{=taom_faction_clans_of_dunland_perk_0_desc}+10% party speed on plains and +5% party size — Dunlending warbands cover ground fast.
{=taom_faction_clans_of_dunland_perk_1_desc}+10% village volunteer respawn rate — villages refill with cousins fast.
{=taom_faction_clans_of_dunland_perk_2_desc}A generations-deep woodland upbringing: 50% less forest speed penalty + 15% sight, and +20% chance for veteran militia in towns; -10% construction speed.
{=taom_faction_clans_of_forochel_desc}Scattered Orc tribes in the frozen northern wastes near the Ice Bay of Forochel. Savage raiders who prey on the Lossoth and any who venture north.
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_isengard_bonus_3}-15% mounted recruit and upgrade cost (War Wargs)
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_isengard_bonus_6}+10% party speed on plains and swamps (Forced March, Fenland Drillmasters)
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_isengard_bonus_7}+2 Merchant + 1 Artisan + 12 Gang Leader notables in Isengard town (20 total)

{=taom_faction_dominion_of_isengard_desc}Saruman's industrial fortress at Orthanc. The Ring of Isengard runs day and night — Uruk-hai legions, forge-line crossbows, war wargs. Isengard's one town swells to twenty notables: a recruitment hub equal to many cities of Rohan. Saruman's Grip alienates every neighbor.
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_isengard_perk_0_desc}+10% party size limit and +10% march speed on plain and swamp.
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_isengard_perk_1_desc}+15% construction, -20% smithing energy, -15% mounted recruitment cost.
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_isengard_perk_2_desc}Isengard's single town swells to 20 notables — 4 Merchant, 2 Artisan, 14 Gang Leader.
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_isengard_su_2_desc}Fast hit-and-run cavalry of the White Hand.
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_mordor_bonus_0}-60% army influence cost (The Dark Lord's Will)
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_mordor_bonus_4}+10% party speed at night (Creatures of the Dark)
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_mordor_bonus_5}+5% party speed on plains and swamps (Shadow March, Dead Marshes)
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_mordor_bonus_7}+2 Gang Leader notables per town (Black Speech Heralds)

{=taom_faction_dominion_of_mordor_desc}Sauron's Black Land. The Dark Lord's Will lets armies muster at minimal influence cost; Nurn Farmlands feed the hordes; Sauron's Wrath turns raids into slaughter; Creatures of the Dark march faster at night than any free people in daylight. Dark Tribute drains the treasury.
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_mordor_perk_0_desc}Army influence cost reduced by 60% — Sauron's hordes need no consensus.
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_mordor_perk_1_desc}+25% raid damage and +5% party speed on plains and swamps.
{=taom_faction_dominion_of_mordor_perk_2_desc}+10% party speed at night — the eyes of Mordor never sleep.

{=taom_faction_goblins_of_blue_craig_desc}A distinct goblin host of the Blue Mountains (Ered Luin) in the far west, hard by the Grey Havens of Lindon — a realm apart from their Misty Mountains cousins of Goblin Town. Same numberless, ill-armed swarms: weak alone, overwhelming in the mass, and ravenous on the march. They trouble the Elves of the western shore.
{=taom_faction_goblins_of_blue_craig_perk_0_desc}+10% party size and +25% village volunteer respawn — weak but numberless.
{=taom_faction_goblins_of_blue_craig_perk_1_desc}+10% party speed on snow — goblins know every crag and tunnel.
{=taom_faction_goblins_of_blue_craig_perk_2_desc}The horde devours everything — +20% party food consumption.
{=taom_faction_goblins_of_blue_craig_su_0_desc}Numberless bow-armed rabble of the high crags.

{=taom_faction_goblins_of_goblin_town_desc}The teeming goblin-warrens beneath the High Pass of the Misty Mountains. Since the fall of the Great Goblin the tribes have multiplied without number — vast, ill-armed swarms that win by sheer weight and breed faster than any foe can cull them. They run swiftest over the snows of their mountain home, but such hordes are ever ravenous.
{=taom_faction_goblins_of_goblin_town_perk_0_desc}+10% party size and +25% village volunteer respawn — goblins are weak but numberless.
{=taom_faction_goblins_of_goblin_town_perk_1_desc}+10% party speed on snow — goblins know every pass and tunnel of the Misty Mountains.
{=taom_faction_goblins_of_goblin_town_perk_2_desc}Such a horde devours everything — +20% party food consumption.
{=taom_faction_goblins_of_goblin_town_su_0_desc}Massed spear-fodder of the High Pass warrens.
{=taom_faction_golden_realm_of_rhun_bonus_2}-10% mounted recruit and upgrade cost (Steppe Horsemanship)
{=taom_faction_golden_realm_of_rhun_bonus_3}+25% horse, mule, cow, and sheep village production (Herders of the Steppe)

{=taom_faction_golden_realm_of_rhun_desc}The Easterlings of the eastern plains. A deep-rooted steppe cavalry tradition pairs with the Easterling Outriders' speed and the Easterling Host's numbers. Heavy cavalry that arrives in force, bringing tribute as well as spears.
{=taom_faction_golden_realm_of_rhun_perk_0_desc}+10% party speed on steppe — riders of the Sea of Rhun cross the plain fast.
{=taom_faction_golden_realm_of_rhun_perk_1_desc}+5% party size limit — hordes muster in answer to Mordor's call.
{=taom_faction_golden_realm_of_rhun_perk_2_desc}Steppe horsemanship brings -10% mounted cost and +25% animal village production; nomadic governance costs -20% town tax income.

{=taom_faction_havens_of_umbar_desc}The corsair haven and Black Numenorean port-city on the southern bays. Corsair Trade slashes caravan costs, Corsair Glory adds renown, Desert Corsairs march fast across the sands — but Corsair Greed inflates every wage bill.
{=taom_faction_havens_of_umbar_perk_0_desc}-25% caravan cost and +15% tariff income — Umbar prospers on every passing ship.
{=taom_faction_havens_of_umbar_perk_1_desc}+8% renown per battle — the corsair name is sung in every port.
{=taom_faction_havens_of_umbar_perk_2_desc}+10% party speed on desert — Umbar's marches cross sand as easily as sea.

{=taom_faction_high_kingdom_of_lindon_desc}The green land west of the Blue Mountains, last realm of the High Elves on the shores of Middle-earth. From the Grey Havens of Mithlond the white ships sail into the West. Círdan the Shipwright, eldest of the Eldar, keeps the fading light of the Falathrim — wise, few, and each blade irreplaceable. Lindon shares the Falathrim strength of Mithlond.
{=taom_faction_high_kingdom_of_lindon_perk_0_desc}+35% influence awarded on army success — the Wise know how to lead.
{=taom_faction_high_kingdom_of_lindon_perk_1_desc}+20% village hearth growth and -15% party food consumption.
{=taom_faction_high_kingdom_of_lindon_perk_2_desc}+10% party speed in forest and +0.5 settlement loyalty per day.
{=taom_faction_high_kingdom_of_lindon_strength_1}Wise leadership reaps greater influence from victory
{=taom_faction_high_kingdom_of_lindon_su_2_desc}Heavy Falathrim guardian of the Grey Havens.
{=taom_faction_khudorom_of_khand_bonus_1}50% less forest speed penalty + 15% sight range (Woodland Militia)
{=taom_faction_khudorom_of_khand_bonus_2}+20% chance for veteran militia in towns (Hardened Levies)

{=taom_faction_khudorom_of_khand_desc}The Variag of Khand. A tradition of woodland militia blends with the Steppe Charioteers' +10% speed across open ground. Mercenary bands ride for whoever pays the most coin.
{=taom_faction_khudorom_of_khand_perk_0_desc}+10% party speed on steppe — Variag chariots roll fast.
{=taom_faction_khudorom_of_khand_perk_1_desc}Mercenary captains ride for whoever pays — but they keep their cut.
{=taom_faction_khudorom_of_khand_perk_2_desc}Woodland militia habits carry over: 50% less forest speed penalty + 15% sight range and +20% chance for veteran militia in towns; -10% construction speed.
{=taom_faction_khudorom_of_khand_weakness_2}Mercenary captains are loyal to coin, not lord

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_angaladh_desc}The Woodmen of Angáladh live under the western eaves of Mirkwood, where their fathers cleared steads among trees so hard that axes ring on them like iron. King Theodemiro's archers watch the Narrows. The realm stands apart from the War of the Ring, but the shadow in the south of the forest grows every year.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_angaladh_bonus_1}-0.5 settlement loyalty per day (Small Territory Exposure)
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_angaladh_perk_0_desc}+10% party speed on plains, the open ground between the trees and the river.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_angaladh_perk_1_desc}Stands outside the War of the Ring: no alliance and no sworn enemy at the start of a campaign.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_angaladh_su_0_desc}Poleaxe and sword guard of the King's hall.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_angaladh_strength_0}A deep archery line, from the Woodman Bowman to the Master Woodman Archer
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_angaladh_strength_2}No sworn enemy at the start of a campaign
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_angaladh_weakness_2}The shadow of the south of Mirkwood at the border
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_arthedain_bonus_3}+1 settlement loyalty per day (Line of Isildur)

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_arthedain_desc}One of the three kingdoms into which Arnor was sundered. Arvedui's line holds Fornost upon the North Downs and its Rangers keep the roads of Eriador, but Dunland and the orcs of Gundabad press on every border of a realm with too few swords.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_arthedain_perk_0_desc}-20% garrison wage and +1 settlement loyalty per day.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_arthedain_perk_1_desc}+5 party morale. Few as they are, the Dúnedain do not break.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_arthedain_perk_2_desc}+10% party speed on plains, where the Rangers keep the old roads open.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_arthedain_su_0_desc}Two-handed elite guard of the King's citadel.

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_cardolan_desc}The southern of Arnor's three successor kingdoms. Its kings lie in the barrows of Tyrn Gorthad and its riders keep the plains between the Baranduin and the Greyflood. It stands apart from the War of the Ring, but Dunland, the goblins and the orcs of the mountains test its few towns every year.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_cardolan_bonus_0}+10% party speed on plains (Riders of Minhiriath)
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_cardolan_bonus_3}+1 settlement loyalty per day (Line of Eärendur)
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_cardolan_perk_0_desc}-20% garrison wage and +1 settlement loyalty per day.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_cardolan_perk_1_desc}+5 party morale. Few as they are, the Dúnedain do not break.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_cardolan_perk_2_desc}+10% party speed on plains, the open country Cardolan's riders know best.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_cardolan_strength_0}The best horsemen of the three northern realms
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_cardolan_weakness_2}Open plains with Dunland across the Greyflood
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dale_bonus_3}+20% relationship penalty from kingdom decisions (Stubborn Council)
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dale_bonus_6}-0.5 settlement loyalty per day (Small Territory Exposure)

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dale_desc}Bard's rebuilt city beneath Erebor. The rich grain of the Long Lake and a hardy tradition of mustering at low cost pair with the Vale Traders' speed on open ground, though Dale's council can be as stubborn as it is proud. A thriving trade alliance with the Dwarves keeps the city rich and ready.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dale_perk_0_desc}+10% party speed on plains — caravans of Lake-town move fast.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dale_perk_1_desc}Trade with Erebor provides bonus income and arms-supply.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dale_perk_2_desc}The Long Lake's +10% village grain and the Lake-town Muster's -50% army influence cost come together; relationship penalty +20% on kingdom decisions.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dorwinion_bonus_1}-0.5 settlement loyalty per day (Small Territory Exposure)

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dorwinion_desc}The vintners of Dorwinion hold the warm slopes above the Sea of Rhûn, and their red wine is prized in every hall that can pay for it. King Hawin rules from Vineholm. The realm stands apart from the War of the Ring, but the Easterlings across the inland sea look harder at its rich, lightly guarded land every year.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dorwinion_perk_0_desc}+10% party speed on plains, along the river roads and the open shore of the inland sea.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dorwinion_perk_1_desc}Stands outside the War of the Ring: no alliance and no sworn enemy at the start of a campaign.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dorwinion_strength_0}A deep bow line, from the Vintner Bowman to the Master of the Vine-bow
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dorwinion_strength_2}No sworn enemy at the start of a campaign
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dorwinion_su_0_desc}Hall guard of the King at Vineholm, the finest foot of the realm.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_dorwinion_weakness_2}Rich land, lightly guarded, with the Easterlings across the sea

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_erebor_desc}The Lonely Mountain reclaimed. Master Smiths cut smithing energy by 30%; Dwarven Honor adds loyalty every day; Dwarven Stubbornness keeps morale unshakable. Slow to build a wall — but the wall holds until the mountain itself falls.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_erebor_perk_0_desc}-30% smithing energy cost — Dwarven forges work twice as fast.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_erebor_perk_1_desc}-25% garrison wage and +1 settlement loyalty per day.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_erebor_perk_2_desc}+5 party morale and +10% village production — Dwarves do not bend.

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_ered_duin_desc}The dwarf-halls of the Blue Mountains at the western edge of Middle-earth. Durin's Folk made Thorin's Halls in their exile, and the Broadbeams and the Firebeards keep Belegost and Nogrod again. They mine iron and sell it to the Elves of Lindon and the Men of Eriador, while the goblins of Blue Craig gnaw at their roads.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_ered_duin_perk_0_desc}-30% smithing energy cost. The forges of Belegost and Nogrod are the oldest in the West.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_ered_duin_perk_1_desc}+5 party morale and +1 settlement loyalty per day.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_ered_duin_perk_2_desc}+10% party speed on snow and +10% village production from the mines of the Blue Mountains.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_ered_duin_su_0_desc}Tower-shield elite of the Broadbeam line, the King's own guard.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_ered_duin_su_2_desc}Axe and shield guard of the capital's gates.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_ered_duin_weakness_2}Few lords, with goblins at the door
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_imladris_bonus_1}+20% village hearth growth (The Last Homely House)

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_imladris_desc}Elrond's hidden valley, sanctuary of the Wise. Elven Wisdom unifies armies at little influence cost; the Last Homely House grows hearths in every village. Elven Pride still drives every council — every Noldor blade is irreplaceable.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_imladris_perk_0_desc}+35% influence awarded on army success — the Wise know how to lead.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_imladris_perk_1_desc}+20% village hearth growth and -15% party food consumption.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_imladris_perk_2_desc}+10% party speed in forest — the trees of Imladris part for their kin.

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_lasgalen_desc}Thranduil's Woodland Realm in northern Mirkwood. Silvan archers and veteran militia hold the great forest against spider, orc, and shadow. Woodland Sustenance keeps the supplies light; Woodland Bonds keep morale high. Forest isolation slows growth.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_lasgalen_perk_0_desc}+10% party speed in forest and -15% food consumption.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_lasgalen_perk_1_desc}+25% chance militia recruits arrive as veterans.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_lasgalen_perk_2_desc}+3 party morale — Silvan elves march with songs.

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_lothlorien_desc}The Golden Wood, realm of Lady Galadriel and Lord Celeborn. Wardens of Lorien defend the mallorn-forests cheaply; Lembas Bread sustains every march; Elven Harmony keeps morale unshakable. Timeless Craft means every change is slow.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_lothlorien_perk_0_desc}+10% party speed in forest and -20% garrison wage.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_lothlorien_perk_1_desc}-15% party food consumption — one bite carries a marching elf a day.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_lothlorien_perk_2_desc}+3 party morale and +0.5 loyalty per day in every settlement.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_lothlorien_su_2_desc}Heavy Elven guardian of the Golden Wood.

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_moria_desc}The orc-host that holds the deep places of the Misty Mountains — the black pits of Moria, won from the Dwarves, and the cold peaks from Caradhras to Methedras. Larger and better-armed than the goblin rabble of the High Pass, they muster vast war-hosts for almost no influence and march hungry but tireless across the snows.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_moria_perk_0_desc}Army recruitment costs 40% less influence — the orc-host needs no consensus to march.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_moria_perk_1_desc}+10% party size and +10% speed on snow — large war-hosts bred to the cold peaks.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_moria_perk_2_desc}A war-host of this size eats greedily — +15% party food consumption.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_moria_su_0_desc}Heavier orc infantry of the deep halls.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_moria_su_1_desc}Bow-orc of the deep halls and high tunnels.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_moria_su_2_desc}Raider bred in the dark of Khazad-dûm.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_neldoreth_desc}An Elven realm in the northern reaches of Mirkwood, where the Wood-elves maintain their ancient forests against the creeping darkness from the south.

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rhudaur_desc}The eastern of Arnor's three successor kingdoms, a hill realm between the Hoarwell and the Loudwater. Its Dúnedain lords hold Cameth Brin and the Angle and rule a hard people of hill-men. It stands apart from the War of the Ring, but trolls walk its fells and the orcs of Gundabad and the mountains watch every pass.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rhudaur_bonus_3}+1 settlement loyalty per day (Line of Eärendur)
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rhudaur_perk_0_desc}-20% garrison wage and +1 settlement loyalty per day.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rhudaur_perk_1_desc}+5 party morale. Few as they are, the Dúnedain do not break.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rhudaur_perk_2_desc}+10% party speed on plains, along the roads the Rangers of the Angle keep open.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rhudaur_su_0_desc}Two-handed elite of the old Dúnedain houses.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rhudaur_su_2_desc}Hill-man with a great axe, hardened in the fells.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rhudaur_strength_0}Fine rangers and a hard two-handed guard
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rhudaur_weakness_0}One town and a handful of hill-holds
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rohan_bonus_2}-15% mounted troop wages (Riders of the Mark)
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rohan_bonus_3}+10% party speed on plains (Riders of the Plains)
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rohan_bonus_6}-10% party speed when over 50% infantry (Cavalry Dependent)

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rohan_desc}The Riddermark of the Horse-lords. Horse-lord Heritage cheapens every mounted recruit and upgrade; Riders of the Mark cuts mounted wages; Horse-lord Fellowship binds the Mark in loyalty. Cavalry Dependent — parties heavy with infantry slow to a crawl.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rohan_perk_0_desc}-15% cost to recruit AND upgrade mounted troops — the Mark trains riders cheaply.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_rohan_perk_1_desc}-15% mounted troop wages and +10% party speed on plains.

{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_south_rhovanion_desc}The Northmen of South Rhovanion ride the wide plains between the southern eaves of Mirkwood and the Sea of Rhûn, horse-breeders and kin of the Éothéod far to the north. King Suniefredo holds Vidugard, and the barrows of the old kings stand on his grasslands. The realm stands apart from the War of the Ring, but the Wainriders have broken it twice before, and the riders of the plains remember it.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_south_rhovanion_perk_0_desc}+10% party speed on plains and +5 party morale: the wide grasslands are the riders' own ground.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_south_rhovanion_perk_1_desc}+0.5 settlement loyalty per day. A host that is mostly foot-soldiers marches 10% slower.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_south_rhovanion_perk_2_desc}Stands outside the War of the Ring: no alliance and no sworn enemy at the start of a campaign.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_south_rhovanion_strength_0}A full cavalry ladder, from the Northman Youth to the Horse-lord
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_south_rhovanion_strength_1}Quick and steady across the open plains
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_south_rhovanion_strength_2}No sworn enemy at the start of a campaign
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_south_rhovanion_su_1_desc}Veteran captain of the riders of the plains.
{=taom_faction_kingdom_of_south_rhovanion_weakness_2}The old Wainrider road lies open in the East
{=taom_faction_overlordship_of_dol_guldur_bonus_4}+1 Merchant + 1 Artisan + 13 Gang Leader notables in Dol Guldur town (20 total)

{=taom_faction_overlordship_of_dol_guldur_desc}The Necromancer's southern hold in Mirkwood. Shadow Command rallies hordes at almost no influence; Dark Conscription drills militia veterans; Shadow Captains swell the one town to twenty notables. Voracious Hordes eat as much as they slay.
{=taom_faction_overlordship_of_dol_guldur_perk_0_desc}Army influence cost reduced by 50% — dread compels obedience.
{=taom_faction_overlordship_of_dol_guldur_perk_1_desc}+5% party size and +20% volunteer respawn rate.
{=taom_faction_overlordship_of_dol_guldur_perk_2_desc}Dol Guldur's single town fields 20 notables — a 15 Gang Leader recruitment hub.
{=taom_faction_overlordship_of_gundabad_bonus_6}+1 Artisan + 3 Gang Leader notables per town (Bone-Smiths, Pale Warband Chieftains)

{=taom_faction_overlordship_of_gundabad_desc}Mount Gundabad, sacred to the Pale Orcs of Bolg's lineage. Vast warbands march from the high passes — Orc Horde discipline rallies hosts for almost no influence, Mountain Marauders rule the snows, and Plunder Demands keep every warlord paid.
{=taom_faction_overlordship_of_gundabad_perk_0_desc}Army influence cost reduced by 40% — dread compels obedience.
{=taom_faction_overlordship_of_gundabad_perk_1_desc}+5% party size limit and +10% party speed on snow.
{=taom_faction_overlordship_of_gundabad_perk_2_desc}+3 Gang Leader and +1 Artisan notable per town — recruitment swells with raiders.
{=taom_faction_overlordship_of_gundabad_weakness_2}Dwarves and Elves hate the Pale Orcs
{=taom_faction_remnants_of_angmar_desc}The dread realm of the Witch-king of Angmar in the far north. From his fortress of Carn Dum, the Witch-king wages war upon the remnants of Arnor.
{=taom_faction_stewardship_of_gondor_bonus_0}+10% party speed on plains (Men of the Fields)
{=taom_faction_stewardship_of_gondor_bonus_5}+1 settlement loyalty per day (Tower Guard Discipline)

{=taom_faction_stewardship_of_gondor_desc}The last bastion of the Dunedain in the south. Tower Guard hold the line, Gondorian Discipline rallies armies cheaply, and the Men of the Fields march on plains. War-Depleted Lands grow slowly — but Gondor stands.
{=taom_faction_stewardship_of_gondor_perk_0_desc}-20% garrison wage and +1 settlement loyalty per day.
{=taom_faction_stewardship_of_gondor_perk_1_desc}+5 party morale and +30% army influence awarded on success.
{=taom_faction_stewardship_of_gondor_perk_2_desc}+10% party speed on plains and +2.5% party size — the Pelennor is open ground.
{=taom_faction_stronghold_of_ered_gwaer_desc}A region dominated by savage Orc tribes from the eastern mountains. Fierce raiders who terrorize the borderlands between Khand and Harad.
{=taom_faction_stronghold_of_narager_desc}A desolate eastern region overrun by Orc tribes. These savage bands raid the borderlands and serve as scouts for the forces of darkness.
{=taom_faction_taskralan_of_harwan_bonus_0}+10% party speed on desert (Sons of the Sun)
{=taom_faction_taskralan_of_harwan_bonus_2}-30% caravan build cost + -10% trade penalty (Desert Caravan Trade)

{=taom_faction_taskralan_of_harwan_desc}The Haradrim of Harwan, sons of the sun. A long desert heritage underlies the Sons of the Sun +10% speed bonus and the Haradrim Warbands' larger numbers, built on a thriving caravan economy. Mumakil rule the southern plains.
{=taom_faction_taskralan_of_harwan_perk_0_desc}+10% party speed on desert — born to burning sands.
{=taom_faction_taskralan_of_harwan_perk_1_desc}+5% party size limit — tribal warbands ride together to Mordor's call.
{=taom_faction_taskralan_of_harwan_perk_2_desc}Desert Caravan Trade (-30% caravans, -10% trade penalty) and Desert-Born (no desert speed penalty) carry over; +5% daily wages.
{=taom_faction_wildmen_of_enedwaith_desc}The wild lands of Enedwaith between Arnor and Gondor. Home to scattered clans of Men who answer to no king, living as hunters and herders.

{=taom_str_culture_description.goblin}The Goblins of the Misty Mountains and the Ered Luin are among the most numerous and persistent of Orc-kind in the West. Dwelling in lightless tunnels beneath the deep roots of the Hithaeglir or high up in the Blue Crag, they are a subterranean folk, more cunning than bold and more treacherous than disciplined. Unlike the hosts of Mordor or the war-bands of Gundabad, Goblins favor ambush, traps and overwhelming numbers. Their halls are crude yet sprawling, carved into the living rock and filled with forges, pits and crooked passageways known only to them. They delight in cruel sport and petty tyranny, squabbling constantly among themselves unless held in check by a particularly fearsome Great Goblin. Small in stature but quick in movement, Goblins are adept at navigating darkness and narrow ways. They raid caravans that brave the mountain passes and descend without warning upon isolated settlements. Rarely unified for long, they are nonetheless dangerous in their own domain. The mountains have devoured many travelers - and the laughter that echoes in their depths is seldom friendly.

{=taom_str_culture_description.mistymountainorcs}The Orcs of the Misty Mountains are a brutal and numberless host of the high peaks. Led by their warlords, they wage endless raids on the lands below, relentless in their cruelty and their hunger for conquest.

{=taom_str_culture_description.cardolan}The Dúnedain of Cardolan hold the south of old Arnor, the plains and river country between the Baranduin and the Greyflood. Their kings lie in the barrows of Tyrn Gorthad, their barges still come up to Tharbad, and their riders are the best of the three northern kingdoms. Their towns are few and their lords quarrel with Arthedain and Rhudaur over the old crown, while the wild lands grow bolder every year.

{=taom_str_culture_description.rhudaur}Rhudaur is the hill kingdom of old Arnor, between the Hoarwell and the Loudwater. Its Dúnedain lords hold the Angle and the tower of Cameth Brin and rule a people of hill-men who never loved the West. The line of its first king still endures, but its holds are cold, its fells are full of trolls, and the orcs of the mountains watch every pass.

{=taom_str_culture_description.eredluin}The dwarves of Ered Luin dwell in the Blue Mountains at the western edge of Middle-earth. Durin's Folk came there in exile and made Thorin's Halls, and in this age the Broadbeams and the Firebeards keep Belegost and Nogrod again, the oldest dwarf-cities of the West. They are miners and smiths, poorer than their kin in the east, and they trade iron with the Elves of Lindon and the Men of Eriador while the goblins of Blue Craig gnaw at their roads.

{=taom_str_culture_description.anduinvale}The Beornings keep the upper vale of the Anduin between the Misty Mountains and Mirkwood, a folk of farmers, herdsmen and honey-keepers who share the river meadows with the Woodmen of the Vales. They hold the Carrock and the Old Ford, take no toll from honest travellers and a heavy one from orcs and wolves. Their chieftains are chosen for strength and plain speech, and they follow no king into a war that is not their own.

{=taom_str_culture_description.angaladh}The Woodmen of Angáladh live under the western eaves of Mirkwood, where their fathers cleared steads among trees so hard that axes ring on them like iron. They are bowmen, woodcutters and hunters, few in number and slow to trust, at peace with the Elves of the northern wood. Every year the shadow in the south of the forest grows, and every year their king sends more of his archers to watch the Narrows.

{=taom_str_culture_description.dorwinion}Dorwinion may very well be one of the most lush and beautiful places in all of Middle-earth. Or so the Dorwinrim say at least. 'Land of Wine' is what their realm is officially referred to, though the mixed society of Elves and Men usually refers to it by its Sindarin calling. Great vinyards line much of the countryside and stretch across hill and dell alike. Bordering them in the east is the Golden Realm of the Medlókan, Easterlings under the sway of Sauron. Great vinters and winemakers, cooks and renowned for their cavalry, the Dorwinrim are the easternmost bulwark against the grasp of the Dark Lord. Due to its lucrative location along the Great Rhûn Road, one of the chief trading routes in Middle-earth, Dorwinion has grown immensely rich and powerful and has, for many centuries now, had a close friendship with both the Avari of Neldoreth as well as the Men of Dale. Friendships, that might be called upon sooner rather than later.

{=taom_str_culture_description.southrhovanion}The Northmen of South Rhovanion ride the wide plains between the southern eaves of Mirkwood and the Brown Lands, a free people of horse-breeders who count the Éothéod of the north as their kin. Their fathers were the lords of the Northmen in the days of the old kings, and the barrows of those kings still stand on the grasslands. Twice the Wainriders came out of the East with wagon and fire and broke them, and the riders of the plains have not forgotten it.

In the campaign, the attacker who takes D sends the defenders back to the lord's hall, and taking the hall's last room (point E) wins the castle. In a Custom Battle, taking D wins the battle. {=taom_mcm_bld_EnableBattleLoadDiagnostics_hint}Logs the full attack->battle-playable lifecycle (encounter, scene selection, Mission.Initialize, every initial-spawn agent's equipment + collision-mesh names) to the TAOM debug log. Leave ON while diagnosing the intermittent battle-load hang — the LAST line in the log names the stuck phase / agent.

{=taom_mcm_bld_EnableExitStallSampler_hint}If a mission exit stalls past 15s, briefly suspends the game's main thread (at +15/+30/+60s) to photograph its call stack into the TAOM debug log — this is what root-caused the tournament-exit freeze (#331). Tiny residual risk: a suspension landing mid-GC can freeze the game harder than the stall itself. Turn OFF to keep the other diagnostics without any thread suspension. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_bld_EnableMissionTickStallSampler_hint}If a battle frame stops for 10s (the agent AI tick or the main mission frame never finishes: the game freezes with no crash), briefly suspends the stuck thread at +10/+20/+40s to photograph its call stack into the TAOM debug log as [MissionStall]. It never runs while the game is responsive, and never while a mission is ending or exiting (the exit sampler above covers that). Independent of the master Battle Load Diagnostics toggle: this is crash forensics, not load logging. Same tiny residual risk as the exit sampler. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_bld_EnableMemorySampler_hint}Writes memory telemetry to the TAOM debug log: a periodic [MemSample] line (process private/working-set MB, managed heap, system commit use/limit, available RAM), a one-shot WARN when system commit headroom runs low, and a [MemStation] line each time a screen opens or closes so growth can be attributed to a screen. This ONE switch governs all three. Independent of the master Battle Load Diagnostics toggle: this is session-wide crash forensics, not battle-load phase logging. Default ON.
{=taom_mcm_bld_MemorySampleIntervalSeconds_hint}Seconds between [MemSample] lines. Default 30s (~120 lines per hour of play). Takes effect on the next sample — no restart needed.

{=taom_mcm_bld_EnableMissionPerfHeartbeat_hint}Writes a [MissionPerf] line to the TAOM debug log every 5 seconds while a mission runs: frames, fps, average / p95 / max frame time in ms, agent and formation counts, garbage collections, and the engine's main-thread and render-thread busy times (mainMs, renderMs). This is the in-mission counterpart of [MemSample] and the measurement an AI or content change is judged against. Cost is one timestamp and one GetMainFps read per frame. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_bld_EnableTickProfiler_hint}Off by default. Adds per-type attribution to the hitch probe's lines: times every mission behaviour's tick, every behaviour's spawn callback and every scene script component by type, and lists the slowest. Installed once at game start: turning it on takes effect after a restart; turning it off stops it from the next mission.

{=taom_mcm_bld_TickProfilerTopN_hint}How many entries each [TickProfile] and [TickSummary] line lists (mission behaviours) and each [MapProfile] and [MapProfileSummary] line lists (map tick listeners and TAOM map views), slowest first. Default 8. Read at each mission start and each campaign session start.

{=taom_mcm_bld_HitchThresholdMs_hint}A frame that takes this many milliseconds or more writes one [Hitch] line naming where the frame went, for the first 100 such frames of a mission; later ones are only counted. Below the battle's usual frame time, nearly every frame is a hitch. Default 250. Read at each mission start.

{=taom_mcm_bld_EnableHitchProbe_hint}On by default. Times the parts of every mission frame TAOM can see (the wait for the agent tick, the mission tick, the camera and render preparation, scene scripts, agent spawns) and checks whether an animation clip is loading from disk, so each frame slower than the hitch threshold writes a hitch line and a detail line saying where the time went. Its measured cost is written to the TAOM debug log. Installed once at game start: turning it on takes effect after a restart; turning it off stops measuring from the next mission while 'Enable Tick Profiler' is off (the profiler measures through the probe's patches).

{=taom_mcm_bld_EnableAnimMemoryProbe_hint}Writes an [AnimMem] line to the TAOM debug log every 5 seconds while a mission runs: how much on-demand animation clip data the engine holds against its 12 MiB budget, whether a clip is loading from disk at the moment of a sample, and how often the total fell between one-second samples (a sign that clips were evicted), plus a summary when the mission ends. Read-only: it finds the two engine values once per game session by a signature check, then once a second reads the clip byte total and asks the engine whether a clip is loading; if the check fails on this game version it turns itself off and says why in the log. Takes effect at the next mission start. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_bld_EnableMapProfiler_hint}Off by default. Times the campaign map's frame: the campaign tick, every per-frame tick-event listener by its owner, the map screen and TAOM's map views, and TAOM's application tick. Writes a [MapProfile] line to the TAOM debug log every 5 seconds while the map runs and a [MapProfileSummary] line when the campaign ends. Turning it on takes effect after a restart (the profiler is installed once, at game start); turning it off stops measuring from the next campaign session.

{=taom_mcm_bld_CullHiddenNameplates_hint}The campaign map updates every settlement nameplate every frame (about a thousand in TAOM), hidden ones included. When on, a nameplate that is hidden and cannot become visible this frame (out of height range, not tracked, not in range, nothing about its settlement changed) is left alone, which saves frame time on the map, most in fast forward. Everything else updates exactly as in the vanilla game. Takes effect on the next frame, so it can be switched with the map profiler on to compare the [MapProfile] lines. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_bld_ReleaseMapViewMemory_hint}In the measurement this feature is adapted from, every screen or menu that covered the campaign map left three colour targets and one depth target of the map view's old set behind (tens of megabytes of graphics memory per closed screen, more at a high resolution). That memory stays until a battle, or a town, village or training grounds scene, starts. When on, every Nth cover (see Map View Release Interval) has the map view release its graphics memory as you return to the map. The map then shows a short loading screen until its view is ready again, on one return in N (about 0.4 s instead of 0.08 s in that measurement). Takes effect at the next cover. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_bld_MapViewReleaseInterval_hint}Release the map view's memory on every Nth cover of the map. Default 20. A lower number gives memory back sooner but shows the short loading screen on more returns to the map (about 0.4 s in the measurement this feature is adapted from); 1 releases on every cover. Takes effect at the next cover.

{=taom_mcm_bld_EnableLoadTimeStamps_hint}Writes the detailed load-time lines to the TAOM debug log: one [PatchApply] line per Harmony patch group with its apply time (written at game initialization), [LoadPhase] steps of TAOM's game start and game initialization, and [Lifecycle] lines timing every campaign handler of a new game, a loaded save and the session start (a line for each handler taking 10 ms or more, and a total per event). The per-type [LoadXml] lines, the patch phase totals and one [Lifecycle] dispatch line per campaign dispatch are always written. Costs a few microseconds per handler while a campaign loads and nothing during play. Default OFF.

{=taom_mcm_bld_LogScreenOpenTimes_hint}Writes one [ScreenOpen] line per screen open to taom_debug.log, naming the screen, the phase and the milliseconds it took. Use it to compare a Fast Open switch off against on. Default OFF.

{=taom_mcm_bld_ClanFastOpen_hint}Opens the Clan screen faster by building its parties list once instead of three times. Turning it off restores vanilla's build for this screen. Read on every open. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_bld_InventoryFastOpen_hint}Opens the Inventory and trade screen faster by skipping work the screen repeats. Turning it off restores vanilla's build for this screen. Read on every open. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_bld_PartyFastOpen_hint}Opens the Party screen faster by caching lookups the screen repeats for each troop. Turning it off restores vanilla's build for this screen. Read on every open. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_bld_QuestLogFastOpen_hint}Opens the Quest log faster by building finished quests only when you select them. Turning it off restores vanilla's build for this screen. Read on every open. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_blow_EnableBlowDiagnostics_hint}Turn ON only to reproduce a combat or siege crash. Logs every damaging blow, every death, and every siege-engine shot to the TAOM debug log (Logs/taom_debug_*.log) with durable flushing, so the LAST line survives a hard native crash and names the fatal blow — victim race, blow flags, damage type, whether it was a fire pot. Costs a synchronous log write per hit while ON, so leave OFF for normal play. Default OFF.

{=taom_mcm_crash_EnableCrashCapture_hint}Master toggle. When off, every TAOM crash finalizer passes exceptions straight through and the AppDomain hook ignores them, so the game's own handler takes over (BUTR's too, unless TAOM already suspended it this session; then restart). Takes effect immediately: the finalizers are always installed at launch and check this toggle only when an exception arrives. Default ON.
{=taom_mcm_crash_SuspendButterLibHandler_hint}On first capture, calls ButterLib.ExceptionHandlerSubSystem.Disable() so TAOM's report wins. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_crash_EnableNativeToManagedCapture_hint}Logs and survives exceptions thrown inside a short list of native-to-managed callbacks (screen early, late and input ticks, scene-script ticks, thumbnail and tableau rendering, and mission combat callbacks for hits, blocks, missiles, charges, falls and agent removal) instead of crashing. When off, those exceptions pass straight through. Takes effect immediately. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_crash_SurviveMissionStartFailures_hint}When a mission behavior, a module's mission-start callback or a mission object throws in one of the six start calls of Mission.AfterStart while a mission is loading, log it, show a short message, cut that call short and let the mission start, instead of the game loading the mission again every frame for ever. A throw elsewhere in the load, such as a behavior's OnMissionScreenPreLoad, is not covered. Enable Crash Capture does not affect this setting. When off, the exception passes straight through as in the vanilla game. Takes effect immediately. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_crash_SkeletonBufferGuard_hint}The engine reserves room for the skeletons drawn in each frame in two per-frame buffers (65,536 and 262,144 entries) and never checks that the next one fits; one skeleton too many (about 2,340 in view for the first buffer) freezes the battle for good. When on, TAOM bounds-checks both buffers by rewriting 13 bytes of the engine at launch at each one, so a skeleton that would not fit is drawn from that buffer's first slots instead (its bones may look wrong for that frame). TAOM installs each check only where the exact engine bytes are found exactly once: a build that only moves the function is still patched, and a changed build gets nothing written. It also writes nothing for a buffer another module already guards, and guards the other one regardless. Takes effect at the next launch. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_crash_SkeletonBufferWatch_hint}Reads how full those two buffers get during every mission, not only battles, and writes the peaks to the log when the mission ends, with how many times each guard had to step in. If nothing guards the first buffer, also shows one warning at 90 percent full. Takes effect at the start of the next mission. Default ON.
{=taom_mcm_crash_WriteCrashBundle_hint}Produces Logs/taom_crash_<timestamp>_<sig>.zip containing report.txt, report.json, taom_debug.log, rgl_log.txt, manifest.txt. Default ON.

{=taom_mcm_crash_MakeBugReportAction_hint}Writes one zip in the Logs folder with what a bug report needs: this game's and the previous game's TAOM logs, the game's own logs, the game's crash folder from the previous game (files up to 64 MB each, 128 MB in all), the module list, the TAOM settings and, in a campaign, the campaign details. Then shows where the zip is. It carries your PC's name, your hero's name and folder paths of your install.
{=taom_mcm_crash_OfferBugReportAfterUnexpectedEnd}Offer A Bug Report After An Unexpected End

{=taom_mcm_crash_OfferBugReportAfterUnexpectedEnd_hint}On the first main menu after a game that closed without TAOM's normal shutdown (a crash, a freeze you had to close, or a stopped game), ask whether to make a bug report from that game's logs. Default ON.
{=taom_mcm_crash_ThrowOnNextMissionTick_hint}QA only. Throws a tagged TaomDevTriggerException on the next Mission.Tick to exercise the crash capture pipeline. Auto-resets to OFF after firing.

{=taom_mcm_crash_ThrowOnNextApplicationTick_hint}QA only. Throws a tagged TaomDevTriggerException on the next Module.OnApplicationTick to exercise the capture pipeline without entering a mission. Auto-resets to OFF after firing.

{=taom_mcm_crash_ThrowOnNextMissionAfterStart_hint}QA only. Throws a tagged TaomDevTriggerException from a TAOM mission behavior's AfterStart on the next mission start, the #699 shape. Needs Enable Crash Capture on. With Survive Mission Start Failures on, the mission starts with that behavior's AfterStart cut short, and one message shows. With it off, the throw escapes once, TAOM's crash capture shows its crash dialog and writes a bundle, and the engine loads the mission again. Auto-resets to OFF after firing.
{=taom_mcm_ShowAllEncyclopediaCharacters_hint}Reveals all characters in the encyclopedia, including those not yet encountered. Equivalent to the 'campaign.toggle_information_restrictions' cheat.

{=taom_mcm_EnableTroopWeight_hint}Weighted party size: elite units consume more party capacity. Elites 2x, level 41+ elites 3x, warg riders 2x, cave trolls 4x, mumakil 10x. This is the default for new campaigns: each campaign keeps its own choice from the start screen, and older saves follow this setting.

{=taom_mcm_EnableAiPartyScaling_hint}Lets AI lord parties HOLD the roster their party template spawns them with. Without this they spawn at 500-3000 and are trimmed back to the vanilla 50-150 cap within a day. Also relieves AI food and wage pressure, because those drive a second, morale-based desertion path that ignores the cap entirely. Off restores the pre-feature behaviour. Note that is not the same as raw vanilla: the Troop Weight elite tax has its own toggle and still deflates a heavy party's limit when it is on. This is the default for new campaigns: each campaign keeps its own choice from the start screen, and older saves follow this setting.

{=taom_mcm_AiLordPartyScale_hint}Multiplies an AI lord's party size limit. Preserves clan-tier progression, so a tier-4 lord still outgrows a tier-1. 1.0 = vanilla, which is the default: this feature ships neutral and you opt in. Raise this and the Flat Bonus together: the bonus is added after the multiplier, so moving one alone shifts the total by less than you expect. Saved values from before November 2026 were reset to this default; if you had chosen your own, set it again.

{=taom_mcm_AiLordPartyFlatBonus_hint}Added to an AI lord's party size limit AFTER the multiplier, so it is worth exactly this many men. Exists because template spawn size does not scale with clan tier: under a multiplier alone, low-tier lords still shed. Default: 0. Saved values from before November 2026 were reset to this default; if you had chosen your own, set it again.

{=taom_mcm_AiGarrisonScale_hint}Multiplies every settlement garrison's size limit, player-owned included. Siege balance, not an AI handicap: lords fielding thousands would walk over garrisons still capped near vanilla's 200. Raising this also gives lords more room to donate troops on entering a friendly fief. 1.0 = vanilla, which is the default. IMPORTANT: raise this only alongside the AI Lord multiplier above. Vanilla refuses to even target a settlement when the attacker is under twice the defender's strength, and that strength counts garrison AND militia, so a high garrison multiplier with vanilla-sized lord parties stops AI sieges happening at all. Saved values from before November 2026 were reset to this default; if you had chosen your own, set it again.

{=taom_mcm_AiPartyFoodRelief_hint}Fraction of an AI lord party's food consumption waived. A large party cannot buy 30 days of food from any town, so it starves permanently, and starvation is -30 morale which opens vanilla's morale-desertion path. 0 = vanilla, which is the default. Only worth raising if you have raised the AI Lord multiplier: at vanilla party sizes nothing starves. Saved values from before November 2026 were reset to this default; if you had chosen your own, set it again.

{=taom_mcm_AiPartyWageRelief_hint}Fraction of an AI lord party's wage bill waived. AI clan wage budgets are set from clan gold and a large party blows past them, pinning unpaid wages at -20 morale and opening the same desertion path. 0 = vanilla, which is the default. Only worth raising if you have raised the AI Lord multiplier. Saved values from before November 2026 were reset to this default; if you had chosen your own, set it again.

{=taom_mcm_AiPlayerClanPartyScaling_hint}Whether YOUR clan's lord parties get the same size scaling as AI lords. 'Taken-over lords only' (default) applies it when you started as an existing lord via Player Switcher, whose clan was given AI-sized rosters at world generation and would otherwise shed thousands of men. Detected from the player clan's id, so it survives save/load. 'Always' also applies it to an ordinary campaign start. 'Never' is the pre-2026-09-01 behaviour. Food and wage relief are never granted to your clan either way.

{=taom_mcm_EnableSettlementFoodTuning_hint}Corrects garrison food consumption (Troop Weight no longer inflates it for elite garrisons) and applies the tunable food knobs in settlement_food/settlement_food_config.json (consumption divisors, base/village/flat production, storage caps). Off = vanilla engine food math (garrison food stays weighted). Config edits need an app restart.

{=taom_mcm_EnableSettlementEconomyTuning_hint}Regenerates town market gold toward a higher target (base 25000 vs vanilla 10000) so drained town markets recover — tunable in settlement_economy/settlement_economy_config.json (base, gold per prosperity, daily regen rate). Applies to existing saves immediately. Off = vanilla engine gold math. Config edits need an app restart.

{=taom_mcm_EnableCaravanTrade_hint}Makes AI/player caravans range beyond the local town cluster instead of shuttling between very-close towns, trade across the endless Free-vs-Evil war (per War Trade Policy below), and carry fuller baskets. Off = exact vanilla caravan behavior. Advanced curve knobs live in caravan_trade/caravan_trade_config.json; config edits need an app restart.

{=taom_mcm_CaravanTradeApplyToPlayer_hint}When on, your OWN caravans also range further, trade cross-war, and buy fuller baskets (they may enter contested territory and risk attack). Off scopes the selection re-weight + basket diversity off your clan's caravans. Note: the wider distance ceiling is engine-global (shared by all caravans) and the war-trade gate scopes at your whole faction, so those two levers aren't fully isolated to non-player caravans — but with this off your caravans still route by vanilla's nearest-first selection.
{=taom_mcm_CaravanRangeMultiplier_hint}How much further caravans range past the vanilla distance ceiling. 1.0 = vanilla reach; higher = they visit more distant, more profitable markets. Default: 1.6.

{=taom_mcm_CaravanWarTradePolicy_hint}Which towns caravans may trade with despite the war. Vanilla = war blocks trade (the cause of the shuttle). Same Side + Neutral = trade with same-alignment or neutral factions but not the enemy side (default, lore-friendly). Ignore War = trade anywhere non-besieged.

{=taom_mcm_CaravanBudgetDiversityFloor_hint}Raises poor caravans' buying power so they stock several goods instead of one. 0 = vanilla (poor caravans buy a single item); higher = fuller baskets. Default: 0.35.

{=taom_mcm_EnableCastleRecruitment_hint}When enabled, castles gain notables with recruitable volunteers — the player can 'Recruit troops' at any accessible castle. Existing notables remain in the save if you later disable this.
{=taom_mcm_EnableCastleRecruitmentAi_hint}When enabled, AI lord parties also score, travel to, and recruit volunteers from castles like they do from towns. Requires Enable Castle Recruitment.
{=taom_mcm_CastleNotablesPerCastle_hint}How many recruiters each castle is populated with (vanilla towns = 5, villages = 3). Higher = more recruitment volume per castle. Default: 3.

{=taom_mcm_EnableEliteEmissary_hint}At a faction's key settlements (capitals), speak with the faction emissary to buy that faction's elite troops for its special resource (Castar, War Spoils, Gems...). Conquering a settlement flips its offerings to the new owner.
